analysis.one_liner: Gives federal regulators power to force recalls of contaminated meat, poultry, and food and fine companies that violate safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: after being introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in June 2006, it received no further action before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, federal law did not clearly require companies to tell regulators when they suspected contaminated food, and the government had no power to force a recall of meat or poultry — recalls were voluntary. This bill would have required anyone in the food supply chain to notify the government of suspected adulterated or misbranded products, let the Agriculture Secretary order recalls and pull inspectors from repeat-violation plants, and let regulators impose civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day (up to $500,000 for companies handling other foods). The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or a hearing in the Senate Agriculture Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers, who would get faster warning and removal of contaminated meat, poultry, and other food from stores, and state and local health officials, who would be notified directly of safety findings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Food consumers and public health officials

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone other than a household consumer who has reason to believe meat, poultry, or food is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of Agriculture or Health and Human Services as soon as practicable [S2][S3].

Gives the Agriculture Secretary authority for voluntary and mandatory nondistribution and recall, including taking control of the product if a company does not act, and directing notice to consumers and state and local health officials [S2][S3].
Lets the Secretary refuse or withdraw inspection from plants with willful or repeated violations, which halts their ability to ship product [S3].

Allows civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation, with each day of a continuing violation counted as a separate offense, and up to $500,000 per act for companies violating food safety provisions; unpaid penalties can be collected through the Attorney General [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors and other food companies, which would bear recall costs, mandatory notification duties, record-disclosure requirements, and exposure to civil penalties.

drawbacks.text: Companies would bear the cost of mandatory recalls and new notification and recordkeeping duties; the bill counts each day of a continuing violation as a separate offense, so penalties could accumulate quickly, and while the bill requires a hearing before penalties, smaller firms have less capacity to manage compliance [S3].

Recalls handled by government order can be slower than a cooperative company-led recall in some cases, and the bill's process of a stop-distribution order followed by a hearing within two business days and then a possible recall order builds in procedural steps before a full mandatory recall takes effect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — faster removal of contaminated food from store shelves and real financial consequences for repeat violators — falls mainly on consumers; the cost falls mainly on the food industry in recall expenses, compliance paperwork, and penalty exposure. The bill includes due-process steps (hearings, judicial review, penalty amounts scaled to business size and culpability) that blunt the heaviest burdens, though mandatory recall authority would represent a significant new enforcement regime for an industry that had operated largely on voluntary recalls.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in June 2006, and the committee never took it up before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Harkin (D-IA) introduced the SAFER Meat, Poultry, and Food Act of 2006 on June 29, 2006 [S1][S5].
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day it was introduced [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, committee report, or floor vote — appears in the action history for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, so the bill died in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat, poultry, and food companies are better off because the bill died: they avoided mandatory recall authority, forced notification of suspected contamination, potential withdrawal of inspectors from repeat-violation plants, and civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation per day. Consumers did not get the mandated recall and notification protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and food companies that avoided recall mandates

for.name: Sen. Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and support in the record consists of a Democratic sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have given the government power to force recalls of their products, pull inspectors from repeat-violation plants, and fine them up to $100,000 per violation per day — costs they avoided when the bill died [S3].

They would have faced a legal duty to report suspected adulterated food, cease distribution on order, make distribution records available, and pay penalties up to $500,000 per act for violations involving food [S3].
